title: Four more properties the question summons
takeaway: Across four further text properties - British spelling, casual register, plural grammatical number and melancholy tone - the same passage read after a next-word question and after a name-the-property question loads different content into the workspace at identical tokens. In every panel the property's name reaches the J-lens top-10 at more stimulus positions under the naming question, while the model's next-word answer respects the property under both questions.
walkthrough:
This is a live widget rather than a static image. It holds four panels, titled spelling, register, number and tone. Each panel is one property of a text.

Inside a panel the same short passage appears twice. Above the first copy sits a label reading "Next-word question"; above the second, "Property question". Both copies are printed as a chat turn: `Human:` then the question, then the passage in quotation marks, then `Assistant:` and the single word the model produced.

The passage is drawn one tokenizer token at a time, so words split - " lab" and "elled" are two tokens. A token is shaded orange where the property's name reaches the top 10 of the [[j-lens-readout]] at that position, at any layer in the [[workspace-layers]] band. Shading comes in three steps: darkest for rank 1 or 2, mid for rank 3 to 5, faintest for anything below. Hovering a token prints its rank. A line under each copy counts the shaded tokens and names the tokens that counted as the property's label.

### How the comparison is set up

The passage tokens are identical across the two copies of a panel. Only the question before them differs. Any difference in shading is therefore attributable to the question, which is the design of the [[paired-question-protocol]] used in the main text and the point of [[directed-modulation]].

### What the four panels show

In every panel the naming question shades more tokens than the next-word question. Spelling goes from 1 shaded token out of 31 to 7. Register goes from 0 out of 38 to 3. Number goes from 2 out of 22 to 10. Tone goes from 2 out of 35 to 5.

A control is built into the model's own answers. Under the next-word question the model continues the British-spelled passage with "colour" and the plural-subject clause with "abstained". The property is being used to predict the next word either way.

The paper's reading follows: the property is represented and in use under both questions, and what the question changes is only whether its name enters the [[j-space]].

These are four hand-picked stimuli, one trial each, on [[claude-model-family|Claude Sonnet 4.5]]. The figure illustrates the effect rather than measuring it; the appendix section reports no aggregate statistic over these four.

terms.definition: The first panel's property: whether the author writes British or American English. The passage carries British spellings throughout - organised, labelled, recognised, favourite.
The second panel's property: how formal or casual the writing is. The passage is deliberately colloquial - "So yeah, we'd been hanging out at Jake's place all afternoon, just chilling".
The third panel's property: the grammatical number of the clause the passage sets up, singular or plural. The passage ends on "the members", which demands a plural verb.
The fourth panel's property: the mood the passage conveys. The passage is written to read as sad - a grey morning, a house that felt emptier than it had in years.

The condition label above the first copy of each passage. The question is "What word do you think comes next? Answer in one word." - answering it well requires sensitivity to the property but never requires naming it.
The condition label above the second copy of each passage. The question asks for the property by name, so the model must produce the label as its answer.

The chat-turn roles that structure each printed prompt. The `Human:` turn carries the question and then the stimulus passage in quotation marks; the `Assistant:` turn carries the model's one-word reply.
The short passage shown in quotation marks after the question. It is byte-for-byte the same in both conditions of a panel, which is what makes the shading difference attributable to the question.

The unit the passage is drawn in and the unit the lens is read at. Shading is per token, so a word split by the tokenizer can be shaded on one fragment and not the other - for example " lab" shaded while "elled" is not.

The colour key printed under the figure, tying the orange shading to the condition that triggers it: the property's name is among the ten highest-scoring tokens of the J-lens readout at that position.

The position of the property's name in the sorted J-lens readout at a token, shown on hover as "rank 9" or similar. Rank 1 is the top lens token; the shading darkness is a coarse function of this rank.
The middle band of layers over which the readout is scanned for each token. A token is shaded if the property's name reaches the top 10 at any layer in that band, not only at one chosen layer.
The small set of vocabulary tokens that count as the property's name for a panel. A stimulus token is shaded if any member of that set makes the top 10, and the count line prints the set.
The target set for the spelling panel. Any of these four tokens in the lens top-10 counts as the dialect having been named in the workspace.
The target set for the register panel. These are the labels that would describe the passage's style if the model were naming it.
The target set for the number panel. These are the labels for the grammatical number of the clause the passage sets up.
The target set for the tone panel. It includes "melanch", a subword fragment, because the full word melancholy is not a single token in the model's vocabulary.
The count line printed under each copy of a passage. It lists the target set and the number of stimulus positions at which some member of it reached the lens top-10.

The paper's readout method: for each vocabulary token it holds a direction in residual-stream space that disposes the model to say that token, and scoring an activation against all of them gives a ranked list. Here it is applied at every stimulus position.

The region of representation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues acts as the model's workspace. The figure's claim is about what enters it, not about what the model represents overall.

The experimental design this figure instantiates: present one stimulus under two questions, one that uses a property without naming it and one that asks for it by name, and compare the lens content at the identical stimulus tokens.

The workspace property under test in this section: the model can change what its workspace holds in response to instructions or task demands, independently of what it outputs. This figure tests the implicit form, where a question rather than an instruction does the directing.
The model the paper reports by default, and the one behind these readouts. The paper corroborates key results on Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5, but this appendix figure shows one model only.
The model's one-word answer to the next-word question in the spelling panel. It is the British spelling, so the answer uses the dialect even though the dialect's name is nearly absent from the lens.
The model's answer to the spelling panel's property question, "Where do you think the author of this passage is from? Answer in one word."
The model's next-word answer in the register panel, completing "it wasn't even that ___". It fits the casual register without naming it.
The model's answer to the register panel's property question, "How would you describe the style of this passage? Answer in one word."
The model's next-word answer in the number panel, completing "the members ___". The verb form agrees with the plural subject, so the grammatical number is in use.
The model's answer to the number panel's property question, "Is the upcoming clause about one entity or more than one? Answer in one word."
The model's next-word answer in the tone panel, completing "even the clock seemed ___". It fits the passage's mood without naming it.
The model's answer to the tone panel's property question, "What mood does this passage convey? Answer in one word."

The paper's distinction underlying this figure: a representation poised to be put into words if the occasion arises, as opposed to one that merely influences behaviour. The question changes which of the two the property is.

numbers.meaning: Panels in the figure, one per property: spelling, register, number, tone. The appendix adds these four to the two properties shown in the main text, part of speech and tense.
Conditions per panel. Each panel prints the same stimulus twice, once after the next-word question and once after the property question.

The cut-off for shading: a stimulus token is shaded when the property's name is among the ten highest-scoring tokens of the J-lens readout there. A wider cut-off would shade more tokens in both conditions.
The three rank bands the shading encodes. Rank 1 or 2 gets the darkest fill, rank 3 to 5 an intermediate tint, and anything ranked below 5 but still inside the top 10 gets the faintest tint.
Stimulus tokens in the spelling panel - the denominator both of its counts. The passage runs from "She had organised" to the closing quotation mark.

Shaded tokens in the spelling panel under the next-word question. The single hit is on " lab" (of "labelled") at rank 9, the weakest shading band, so the dialect name is at the edge of the top 10 rather than absent outright.

Shaded tokens in the spelling panel under the property question - a seven-fold rise on identical text. Five of the seven are at rank 1, on "She", " the", " lab", "." and the closing quotation mark; the other two are rank 2 on " been" and rank 4 on " the".
Stimulus tokens in the register panel, the longest of the four passages.

Shaded tokens in the register panel under the next-word question. This is the cleanest case in the figure: no informal, casual, colloquial or conversational token enters the top 10 anywhere in the passage, yet the model still answers "bad" in keeping with the register.

Shaded tokens in the register panel under the property question, at " ch" (of "chilling") at rank 1, " fre" (of "freaked") at rank 2, and " hanging" at rank 9. The two strong hits land on the passage's most colloquial words.
Stimulus tokens in the number panel, the shortest of the four passages.
Shaded tokens in the number panel under the next-word question: " through" at rank 9 and the closing quotation mark at rank 2.

Shaded tokens in the number panel under the property question - nearly half the passage. Six sit at rank 1, mostly on function words and punctuation; the rest run at rank 2, 3 and 9. This panel shows the largest shift of the four.
Stimulus tokens in the tone panel.
Shaded tokens in the tone panel under the next-word question: " it" at rank 5 and a comma at rank 8. Both are mid or faint shading, so the mood words sit low in the readout.

Shaded tokens in the tone panel under the property question, at ranks 1 (" The"), 1 (" empt"), 3 (" a"), 4 (" it") and 6 (a comma). The rise here is the smallest of the four panels, roughly two and a half times rather than seven or five.
Trials per cell. Every count in the figure comes from a single forward pass on a single hand-written stimulus, which is why the section reports a pattern rather than a rate.
